1:
Henry marks the progress. After the prophet had observed the courts he was at length brought to the temple, and Henry makes a rule of it: if we attend to the instructions given in the plainer parts of religion and profit by them we shall be led further into the mysteries, and those willing to dwell in the courts of God shall at length be brought into his temple. He adds a personal note, that the prophet was himself a priest but had been cut short by the iniquity and calamity of the times of his birthright privilege of ministering in the temple, and that God made up the loss by bringing him into this one and employing him to describe it to the church, dignifying him above all the rest of his order. Clarke says only that the chapter gives a circumstantial account of the measures and parts and chambers and ornaments.

Henry then works the ambiguity of the word. When the Lord spoke of destroying this temple his hearers understood the second temple at Jerusalem while he spoke of the temple of his body; and Henry says he might well speak so ambiguously, since the vision of this prophet has a joint respect to them both together, and to the mystical body as well, which is called the house of God, and to all its members, who are living temples. Gill reads the temple of the whole gospel church state, and particularly of the latter day, a holy temple built of living stones for the offering of spiritual sacrifices.

The first measurements produce an apparent discrepancy, and Ellicott resolves it. The posts are the parts of the wall at the sides of the entrance; here they are six cubits, but in the next verse the sides of the door are five, and five with the ten of the doorway and five again makes the twenty of the whole width. The measurement of the first verse must therefore be taken the other way, of the thickness of the side walls, which were the same as the other walls; and he notes that the words which was are not in the original and give a false impression, and that tabernacle was the name the sanctuary bore before the temple was built. Wesley makes the same point about the thickness, that these walls took up as much space as the whole breadth of the older tabernacle. Gill observes that this door was twice as broad as the door of the earlier temple.

The inner room draws the finest observation in the chapter. Ellicott notices a change in the usual formula: everywhere else the angel brings the prophet to the place to be measured, but here he goes in alone, because under the law the prophet might not enter the holy of holies; the prophetic vision, he says, was not yet clear enough to speak of the way into the true holy place as at length opened to all. He also distinguishes door as the doorway, the clear space between the posts, from the door itself, which was a cubit broader and overlapped the posts by half a cubit on each side. Keil and Delitzsch judge the height of six cubits to be in fitting proportion. On the dimensions of the inner room Clarke and Ellicott agree that they are exactly those of the earlier temple, an exact cube, and Clarke infers from this and the other resemblances that the two were on the same plan and that the later was meant to be an exact resemblance of the former. Ellicott adds that the thickness of the wall dividing the two rooms is nowhere given and is not taken into the measurements, being merely a division, a veil or a wooden screen occupying little room.
5:
Ellicott begins with the thickness of the wall, the same as that of the outer court, about ten feet: great massiveness is characteristic of eastern architecture, he says, but is carried to excess in this vision in order to set forth the firmness and security of the things symbolised. He also removes a supplied word, since the prophet measured the range of side rooms collectively rather than every chamber, and notes that they surrounded the house except at the front where the porch stood. Keil and Delitzsch treat the same range as the side-chamber building of the house. Gill turns the wall into a figure of the strength of the church, and Wesley traces its thickness diminishing storey by storey.

The chambers are counted three storeys high and thirty in each, ninety in all, and Ellicott renders the Hebrew literally as three, and that thirty times. He compares them with those of the earlier temple, which they match except for being a cubit narrower, and rejects the Greek version, which puts a space between the chambers and the wall of the house: that is inconsistent with the original, would require an inner wall for the chambers of which nothing is said, and leaves no room for one. Gill reports what the historians and the rabbis say, that the earlier temple had thirty in each of three storeys, and that the second temple had thirty-eight, fifteen on the north, fifteen on the south and eight on the west; and Ellicott concludes from the plan that a uniform size requires twelve on each side and six at the end.

The enlarging upward is where the voices diverge. All agree the chambers grew wider as the wall receded to leave a ledge for the beams, which is why, as Clarke and Wesley both note, the beams were not fastened into the wall of the house itself but rested on projections. Gill sets the floors at four, five and six cubits and the wall at six, five and four; Wesley gives five, six and seven for the chambers. Gill draws a figure from it, that the enlargement signifies the church growing wider as it comes nearer the heavenly state, the present state answering to the lowest storey where the chambers are narrowest. Clarke supposes a winding staircase widening as the wall thinned; Wesley has the stairs running up between each pair of chambers with two doors at each landing. Ellicott is franker than any of them: the description is difficult and has called out much variety of opinion, and it is impossible to go into more detail without discussing words whose meaning is disputed.

One phrase gets a small monograph. The words rendered six great cubits are literally six cubits to the joint, or to the armpit, the word bearing both senses. Ellicott rules out the armpit: no cubit of that length is known to have been in use at any time, and the prophet has already fixed the length of his cubit earlier. The sense must therefore be joint, which applied architecturally can only mean the point where one part of the building meets another, here where the superstructure meets the foundation. He then adds up the whole. Across: the wall six, the chambers four, their outer wall five, the platform beyond five, and the open space twenty, making forty on each side, so eighty, and with the twenty of the inner width exactly the hundred cubits of the inner court. Lengthwise, taking the porch as belonging to the court: the inner length sixty, rear wall six, chambers four, outer wall five, platform five and space twenty, again a hundred, so that the whole is an exact square.
12:
What this western building was for nobody knows, and each says so in his own way. Keil and Delitzsch state that nothing more definite about its purpose is given than can be gathered by inference. Henry says frankly that we are not told what use was to be made of it, and offers a guess: in this vision it may signify the setting up of a church among the Gentiles, not inferior to the Jewish temple but of quite another nature, and one that should soon supersede it. Ellicott offers a different guess and a more prosaic one, that it is probably the appointed place named later for burning the sin-offering, and any remains of other sacrifices that had to be consumed by fire, and other refuse from the temple. Wesley notes only that it is a new building not mentioned before and now measured by itself.

The separate place itself is variously identified. Gill takes it for the holy of holies, separated by a wall in this temple and the first and by a veil in the second. Clarke supposes the temple itself is meant. Ellicott makes it the space twenty cubits broad at the west end of the temple, before one comes to the other building.

The measurements are then summed. Ellicott works out the width of the western building at eighty cubits including its two walls, which leaves a passage of ten cubits on each side, and its length at a hundred, which just fills the space from the separate place to the wall of the court. Clarke does his own addition and reaches a hundred and one cubits for the temple from the western wall to the vestibule, itemising five for the separate place, nine for the wall and attached chambers, sixty for the sanctuary and holy place, ten for the vestibule and twelve for the two great walls. Gill and Wesley take the hundred cubits as the sum total of the whole house with its walls. Henry observes that the western building is of equal dimensions with the house and stands in a court by itself.

Ellicott closes with an admission. The rest of the chapter, he says, enumerates details mostly not mentioned before, introduced by a summary of measurements already taken, so that the clause should be read as and he had measured; the only new thing is the galleries. He is certain they belong to the western building, but the word occurs only here and in three other places, its derivation is quite unknown, and though the translation is probably right they are not located definitely enough to be drawn on the plan; since there was a space of ten cubits on each side of that building, there may well have been galleries covering its entrances.
16:
Ellicott spends most of his effort correcting the English. The door posts are thresholds; the narrow windows are rather closed windows; and stories is not in the original at all and introduces a wrong idea, the prophet having measured the three buildings and now giving details of their three constructions. The clause about ceiling with wood is really a parenthesis and scarcely intelligible as it stands: read opposite the thresholds was a ceiling of wood round about, the part strictly opposite the threshold being the lintel, though the phrase is broad enough to take in the sides of the doorway. After the parenthesis the measuring resumes, so that the space between the ground and the windows was measured too, and then it is added that the windows were covered by lattices fastened so as not to be opened. Gill reads the windows spiritually: in the older sanctuaries there were none, God dwelling in thick darkness, whereas here there is much light, narrow without but broad within.

The carving is the one place where the voices differ about substance. Keil and Delitzsch head the passage as treating of the ornamenting of the inside of the sanctuary. Ellicott takes the figures to be carved on the woodwork as in the earlier temple, notes that the plural ending added in English to cherubim is unnecessary since the word is already plural, and explains the two faces where four are given elsewhere by saying that the cherubim, being symbolic rather than actual creatures, may be modified at pleasure and here have two in accordance with the exigencies of the carving. Clarke describes the alternation, a palm tree between each pair, one face turned to the tree on the right and one to the tree on the left. Gill takes the cherubim not for angels at all but for the ministers of the word, distinguished on one side from angels and on the other from ordinary Christians; the face of a man shows they are men and should be humane and kind. Wesley observes only that the descriptions of these figures differ greatly from place to place.

On the posts Gill dwells on their being foursquare, neither round like pillars nor arched above, and reports having heard that those of the earlier temple were the same though he will not vouch for it; almost everything in this building, he says, was foursquare, which denotes the firmness and stability and perfection of what is in it. Ellicott notes that the word for posts here is different from the one used before and always means the framework in which the doors hung, and that the frames of the holy place and the holy of holies were square and just alike.

The wooden altar draws the fullest typology. Gill identifies it as the altar of incense and reads it of the mediation of Christ: it was made of wood, which may signify the human nature, of the earth as wood is yet produced without sin, and it was overlaid with gold, which may denote the deity that gives virtue to the intercession. Ellicott makes the same identification, notes that its dimensions are here enlarged, takes the corners to include the projecting horns which were always an important part of the symbolism, and observes that table and altar are used synonymously. On the doors Gill counts one apiece for the temple and the sanctuary and finds a figure in their unequal breadth, more entering the outward visible church than the state it prefigures; he and Ellicott agree that each door was made in two parts and each part again in two folding leaves. Clarke explains that the planks had to be thick because the cherubim and palm trees were carved in relief out of their substance. Ellicott admits the last item is extremely doubtful, the word occurring elsewhere only once, and suggests a moulding of wood.
